title: Muscular system anatomy: muscle groups and tendons
description: Explore major muscle groups in the overview, then follow the full-body muscle and tendon atlas for hundreds of named records and regional views.

questions.question: How do skeletal muscles move joints?
questions.answer: Skeletal muscle fibers contract and transmit force through tendons or other attachments. When a muscle crosses a joint, its contraction can pull the attached bones; opposing muscles help control the movement.

questions.question: Are all human muscles listed among the overview cards?
questions.answer: No. The overview cards introduce major regions, while the linked full-body muscle and tendon atlas contains hundreds of named records. A single fixed count of muscles varies with naming and counting conventions.

questions.question: Where can I find posterior muscles such as the triceps and hamstrings?
questions.answer: The full-body muscle atlas groups them by arm and thigh region, including deeper layers and sex-specific pelvic floor views. The front-oriented overview image alone cannot identify posterior fibers.

questions.question: What is the difference between a tendon and a ligament?
questions.answer: A tendon transfers muscular force to an attachment, commonly a bone; a ligament connects bones across a joint. Both consist largely of dense collagenous connective tissue but have different mechanical roles.

questions.question: Is the diaphragm a skeletal muscle?
questions.answer: Yes. The diaphragm is a dome-shaped skeletal muscle separating the thoracic and abdominal cavities and is the primary muscle used during quiet inspiration. Its central tendon is an attachment region, not a separate muscle.
